Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

pass for verb

also pass oneself off as, pass someone off as, be taken for

classical

Ter. Eun. 2.3.84: fōrma et aetās ipsast, facile ut prō eunūchō probēs, “pass for one” (Lewis & Short s.v. probō)
Cic. Verr. 2.5.78: quem prō illō probāre vellēs (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 105: pass for (appear to be), probāre prō (+ abl.)

probāre prō (+ abl.)

probāre, transitive: aliquem prō aliquō probāre, to pass someone off as someone; absolutely, prō eunūchō probēs, you’d pass for a eunuch

pass (someone, oneself) off as

Latin makes the impostor the subject of an active verb: you “make (yourself) acceptable as” the other. Probārī in this sense is not quoted by Lewis & Short; Traupman prints the active.

SourcesLewis & Short: probo

John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 105, each phrase checked against the searchable text of the book.

Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
